analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate and gift taxes on inherited wealth.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee in 1997 without ever receiving a House vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have eliminated the federal estate tax, which applies to the value of large estates left at death, and the gift tax, which taxes large transfers made during life. The repeal would have taken effect for deaths and gifts after September 30, 1997. It provided no replacement revenue, so the lost money would have had to be made up by other taxpayers or borrowing. The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of the largest estates — the estate tax in 1997 applied only to estates above roughly $600,000, so the benefit would flow almost entirely to wealthy families passing on substantial assets, including large family businesses and farms at the high end.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals chapter 11 of the Internal Revenue Code, ending the federal estate tax for estates of people dying after September 30, 1997 [S3].
Repeals chapter 12, ending the gift tax on large lifetime transfers made after September 30, 1997 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally. The bill raises no replacement revenue, so roughly the full amount the estate and gift taxes collected — a tax paid only on the largest estates — would be lost from the Treasury and effectively shifted to everyone else through higher deficits or other taxes.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would eliminate the most progressive part of the federal tax code, a tax that by design applies only to the largest estates, and the bill includes no revenue offset [S2, S3].

Supporters of keeping the estate tax argue it limits the growth of concentrated, inherited wealth; repeal would allow unlimited untaxed transfers between generations. (Good-faith supporter objection: estate taxation can force heirs to sell family businesses or farms, though the 1997 exemption already shielded most small estates.) [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a tax cut concentrated on a small number of the wealthiest families, while the cost — the lost federal revenue — is spread across all taxpayers. The bill contains no provision to replace the lost money, so its design is a straightforward transfer of the tax burden from the largest estates to everyone else.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Ways and Means Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mac Thornberry introduced the bill on February 13, 1997, and it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day [S1, S5].
On February 24, 1997, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where it stayed; no further action is recorded for the remainder of the 105th Congress [S5].
The bill attracted 6 cosponsors — 5 Republicans and 1 Democrat — and never reached the House floor [S4, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The estate tax continued to apply to the largest estates; no taxpayer group gained or lost because nothing was enacted. Opponents of repeal kept the status quo intact without ever having to vote on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The existing estate tax simply remained in place

for.name: Rep. Mac Thornberry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the estate and gift taxes.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on February 13, 1997, referred it to a subcommittee, and never reported it out or scheduled a vote.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was overwhelmingly Republican — 5 of the 6 cosponsors were Republicans, with 1 Democrat — and the bill sat in committee controlled by the majority party without action [S4, S5].

industries.note: Repeal would have ended the only federal tax levied specifically on large inherited fortunes, shifting that burden to taxpayers as a whole. The benefit would flow to a small number of very wealthy families.

industries.industry: Owners of large family businesses and farms
industries.note: Repeal would have spared larger family businesses and farms from estate-tax liability, a common argument for repeal. However, the 1997 exemption level already exempted most estates, so the gain here was concentrated in larger operations.
